body_markdown:
Even before WWII ended following Japan’s surrender on August 15th and the historic signing on the deck of the USS Missouri on September 2nd, Ford was converting its wartime aircraft assembly plants back into civilian production. After altering the[Willow Run plant](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/watch-fords-willow-run-plant-churn-out-a-b-24-every-55-minutes/) to out B-24s at a peak of one bomber every 55 minutes, the switch back to sedans and woody wagons must have been quite a shock.


Like other auto manufacturers, Ford’s product reversion brought back most of the same tooling used to make 1942 civilian models, so except for a new grille and fresh bits of trim, the 1946 models that came off the assembly line starting in the summer of 1945 didn’t offer much change. Consumers, who had gone several years without any new cars on the market, didn’t seem to mind.


LBI-Limited


LBI-Limited


This Ford Super Deluxe Station Wagon could have been among those produced in the first few months back. A deeper dive into the serial number could probably sort that out. Like the pre-war woodies, the 1946 models use wood for much of the body structure aft of the firewall, including the roof, doors, and tailgate, with a vinyl covering for the roof. After long-term ownership by the same family since the early ’50s, this well-aged wagon is[now up for sale on Hagerty Marketplace](https://www.hagerty.com/marketplace/auction/1946-Ford-Super-Deluxe/b3cd81bd-e2e8-4299-8647-e9de5f55efed) .


We don’t know when this ration card was placed in the vehicle, although WWII fuel rationing ended before the war officially did.


LBI-Limited


There are still a few bits of a 1952 Cornell University parking pass in the window.


LBI-Limited


After using it to commute to Cornell in the ‘50s, the woody served all sorts of roles for the family, and it drove across the northeast United States through the early ‘90s. After that, it spent the next 30 years in storage. Although this wagon didn’t come to our attention by a chance encounter with our[woody-driving friend Tom Cotter](https://www.hagerty.com/media/videos/barn-find-hunter-takes-his-woody-wagon-to-woody-specialist/) , it does look like it’s just been rolled out from a deep slumber in the back of a barn.


After the wagon’s long-term owner passed away, his heirs have spent the last few years getting it back up and running. Ragtops & Roadsters of Perkasie, Pennsylvania, and Apache Automotive Restorations and Customs of Bristol, Rhode Island, recently gave the Ford a mechanical once-over while preserving the wagon’s well-earned patina. Ragtops & Roadsters replaced the wiring harness, front wheel bearings, and exhaust system, while Apache Automotive Restorations and Customs addressed the steering, suspension, brakes, and tires. They also gave the[flathead V-8](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/fords-flathead-v-8-gave-power-to-the-people/) an ignition tune-up and mounted new tires, so it’s ready for its return to the road after its long retirement.


The original 239ci flathead V-8 was replaced at 90,000 miles at some point in the ‘60s. Service records show that the chassis had racked up 99,518 miles by 1967.


LBI-Limited


While rust isn’t much of a concern for a mostly wood-bodied vehicle, there are other challenges to keeping them in top condition. Thanks to its preservation, this Super Deluxe Station Wagon has kept its original Ford woodwork intact and remains a solid survivor, with its wood structure even outlasting its original flathead V-8. We hope that the new owners are able to show off this time capsule of a wagon and maintain its impressive history for decades to come.

The electrical system has been converted to negative ground, and the gauge cluster has been modified to work as such.
